Fifty-million-pDAI execution and complete reinvestment
30 September 2026. Hypothetical capacity experiment; no live trading.
Specification
The system's proposed policy dedicates every acquired asset and attributable net earning to peg
support. All acquired pDAI is deployed into compatible pDAI/U liquidity positions. Required U is added
alongside it, and other inventory supports surrounding conversion markets, lending liquidity and
operating costs. LP ownership remains usable by the controller unless a separate decision intentionally
relinquishes withdrawal rights.
This policy does not require every asset to be deposited into every venue at once. Aave receipts, their
wrappers and Balancer LP tokens can express nested claims on the same principal. Reserve accounting
records that principal once. Adding pDAI alone increases sell-side availability but is not equivalent to
adding the U that pays future pDAI sellers. Balanced or appropriately targeted deposits determine the
resulting execution capacity.
The experiment tests a single 50,000,000-pDAI sale against liquidity present before the trade. U is
initially valued at $1; a separate $0.80 scenario tests the difference between internal token parity and
dollar execution. Constant product pools charge 0.3% input fees. The two-coin StableSwap model
charges 0.04% output fees and defines Ann = 2A. These A values are normalized model parameters, not a
claim that an arbitrary deployed Curve getter uses the same precision or convention. There is no
controller correction during the sale.

pDAI stabilization thesis · 4 October 2026 281

StableSwap A=100 250m 49,877,212.688687 0.997544 0.995327
StableSwap A=100 500m 49,930,075.410206 0.998602 0.997585
StableSwap A=2000 100m 49,963,362.176383 0.999267 0.998714
A 50m trade is therefore compatible with tight execution under explicit depth, asset-value and pool-rule
assumptions. At A=100, 100m per side satisfies an average 99-cent requirement but leaves the
subsequent small sale below that band. At 250m per side both measurements exceed 99 cents. Average
execution, post-trade marginal conditions and system response time are separate promises.
For a constant-product pool initially holding equal-value reserves R and fee f, the average output ratio
for a sale q is (1−f)R/[R+(1−f)q]. Requiring at least r gives R >= q(1−f)r/[(1−f)−r], where r < 1−f. For q=50m,
f=0.003 and r=0.99, this requires about 7.050214286 billion units per side. This is an average-
execution bound, not a sufficient post-trade quote bound.
With U worth $0.80, the A=100, 100m-per-side case pays only about $39.724320m, despite returning
49.655400m U. Amplification changes price impact around the assumed exchange relationship; it does
not guarantee the external value of U.
Liquidity growth and fee recycling
A second schedule starts with 25m pDAI and 25m U, adding 25m of each per round. These are declared
new inventory inputs obtained elsewhere by the system. After three additions, reserves reach 100m
each; after eight, 225m each. Each checkpoint runs the same 50m sale independently. Checkpoints are
not successive sales whose depleted balances are silently reset.
A separate recycling calculation starts after those eight additions. It grants 40,000 U of settled outside
fee assets, an 80% system entitlement and 2,000 U of costs/reserves, leaving 30,000 U available.
These fees come from outside the tested pool; they are not counted again on top of fees already inside
its reserves.
The controller spends about 15,002.005618 U buying 14,995.994916 pDAI from the pool, then
contributes every acquired pDAI and the remaining 14,997.994382 U in a proportional LP join. All
purchased pDAI is deployed. The final pool holds 225m pDAI and 225.030m U. Its net new pDAI is zero
because the purchase and redeposit used the same pool; its net new U is 30,000. Buying pDAI elsewhere
and depositing here would instead move pDAI between venues.
That example prevents double counting while demonstrating the intended policy: collected outside
income becomes productive liquidity. In a partially owned pool, proportional joining creates new LP
claims and swap fees accrue according to actual ownership. Fee entitlement at inaccessible LP
addresses is not withdrawable system income. Borrowing produces a liability; gross swap turnover does
not itself measure profit.
Slippage and holding through a re-peg
A sale creates a price difference that can reward a subsequent buyer. Immediate arbitrage closes against
a different funded price. Buying discounted pDAI and holding until recovery takes price and timing
exposure. The system may choose that position because its objective spans many transactions. Realized
gains still require a closing sale or a clearly stated valuation basis.
pDAI stabilization thesis · 4 October 2026 282

The returning price is financed through actual trades, reserve allocation or outside demand. It does not
retroactively improve the initiating seller's execution. Reinvesting profits can deepen future liquidity, but
feeding the same assets repeatedly through controlled accounts does not create external earnings. This
is why the proposal must measure retained net output and usable depth rather than the number of
internal transactions.
Reproduction and checks
Run Research/scripts/model_pulsechain_liquidity_growth.py with --manifest Research/experiments/
pulsechain_liquidity_growth_20260930.json and a fresh --output path. Saved results are in artifacts/pulsechain-
liquidity-expansion-20260930/growth-results.json. The output records manifest/script hashes, 15 capacity
cases, nine independent growth checkpoints, fee-recycling balances and the algebraic constant-product
bound. The implementation uses Decimal precision 70 and a quadratic solution for the StableSwap
output reserve. T ests compare it to a separately implemented integer iterative invariant and check the
recycling conservation identities.
pDAI stabilization thesis · 4 October 2026 283
